title: Ames with the British: 'my sins are remitted' is a deduced conclusion, lesser certainty than principles
source_text: CXXXVI. Deinde cum Theologis illis Magnae Britanniae, idem hac in parte sentire Amesium, clare ostendunt ejus verba quae alicubi citat in rem suam vir doctus. Dixerat Bellarminus statum quaestionis de certitudine quam quis habere possit, vel debeat de sua justificatione, & remissione peccatorum suorum, si absque fallacia & ambiguitate constituatur, hunc esse: Utrum debeat, aut possit aliquis, sine speciali revelatione, certus esse certitudine fidei divinae, cui nullo modo potest subesse falsum, sibi esse remissa peccata. Respondet Amesius his verbis: Sine omni fallacia & ambiguitate, non ponitur in hoc statu certitudo fidei divinae; quia non distinguit Bellarminus inter gradus certitudinis hujus, respectu principiorum quae immediate revelantur, & conclusionum ex illis evidenter deductarum, & inter certitudinem fidei in sese & illam quae est ex fide vel in apprehensione, vel in spe. Sed istis ambiguitatibus, admittimus hunc statum quaestionis, & affirmativam partem tuebimur contra Pontificiorum negativam. Sensus Amesii satis manifestus est illis qui sunt in Amesii lectione & doctrina versati, nempe in omnibus, quae dicuntur fide divina credi, non esse parem certitudinis gradum: Nam fide divina creditur non tantum principia immediate revelata, sed etiam conclusiones, quae ex principiis illis evidenter deducuntur; fidem autem non pari cum certitudine versari circa conclusiones & circa principia. Proinde cum haec propositio, mihi sunt remissa peccata, non sit immediate a Deo revelata, sed solum conclusio ex principiis revelatis deducta, fidem minori cum certitudine illam amplecti, quam ipsa principia.
pass_a_gloss: Next, that Ames feels the same on this point with those Theologians of Great Britain, his words which the learned man somewhere cites for his own purpose clearly show. Bellarmine had said that the state of the question concerning the certainty which someone can or ought to have of his justification and the remission of his sins, if it be constituted without fallacy and ambiguity, is this: Whether anyone ought or can, without special revelation, be certain with the certainty of divine faith, to which falsehood can in no way be subject, that his sins are remitted to him. Ames answers in these words: Without all fallacy and ambiguity, the certainty of divine faith is not put in this state; because Bellarmine does not distinguish between the degrees of this certainty with respect to principles which are immediately revealed and conclusions evidently deduced from them, and between the certainty of faith in itself and that which is from faith either in apprehension or in hope. But with those ambiguities removed, we admit this state of the question, and we will defend the affirmative part against the Pontificians' negative. The sense of Ames is plain enough to those versed in reading and doctrine of Ames — namely that in all things which are said to be believed by divine faith there is not an equal degree of certainty: for by divine faith are believed not only principles immediately revealed, but also conclusions which are evidently deduced from those principles; yet faith does not turn with equal certainty about conclusions and about principles. Therefore since this proposition, my sins are remitted to me, is not immediately revealed by God, but only a conclusion deduced from revealed principles, faith embraces it with lesser certainty than the principles themselves.
pass_b_english: Ames aligns with the British: answering Bellarmine's framed question — can one without special revelation be certain with divine-faith certainty that sins are remitted? — Ames says Bellarmine fails to distinguish degrees: principles immediately revealed versus deduced conclusions, and faith-in-itself versus fiducia in apprehension or hope.
Once ambiguities are cleared, Ames defends the affirmative against Rome's denial — but not with equal certainty across all that is called divine faith.
Because 'my sins are remitted' is a deduced conclusion, not an immediately revealed principle, faith holds it with lesser certainty than the principles.
